source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN Examination, 7th ed.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client with myasthenia gravis is started on pyridostigmine. Which side effect should the nurse ask the client about?
questions.rationale: Pyridostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Overstimulation of neuromuscular receptors causes muscle cramps and small muscle contractions.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q8 (PDF p. 145)
questions.quote: Muscle cramps and small muscle contractions are side effects and occur as a result of overstimulation of neuromuscular receptors.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A client with depression is prescribed tranylcypromine, an MAO inhibitor. Which food should the nurse teach the client to avoid?
questions.rationale: MAO inhibitors can cause a hypertensive crisis with tyramine-rich foods: aged cheeses, figs, bananas, sauerkraut, avocados, soybeans, and fermented, smoked, or aged meats and fish.
explanations: Correct: aged cheese is high in tyramine.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q12 (PDF p. 150)
questions.quote: Foods that contain tyramine need to be avoided because of the risk of hypertensive crisis associated with use of this medication.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client with Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia is to receive IV pentamidine. How should the nurse give it safely?
options: Over 1 hour with the client ambulating
Over 1 hour with the client lying supine
As a 5-minute IV push with the client seated
Over 4 hours with the client in high Fowler's
questions.rationale: Pentamidine is infused over 1 hour with the client supine to reduce the risk of severe hypotension and dysrhythmias. BP and cardiac rhythm are monitored.
explanations: Ambulating risks a fall from hypotension.
Correct: infuse over 1 hour, client supine.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q17 (PDF p. 155)
questions.quote: IV pentamidine is an antifungal medication infused over 1 hour with the client supine to minimize severe hypotension and dysrhythmias.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client takes sotalol 80 mg twice daily. Which finding suggests an ADVERSE effect of the drug?
questions.rationale: Sotalol is a beta blocker. Adverse effects include palpitations, bradycardia, irregular heartbeat, difficulty breathing, signs of heart failure, and cold hands and feet.
explanations: Not an adverse effect of sotalol.
Not an adverse effect of sotalol.
Not an adverse effect of sotalol.
Correct: palpitations signal a cardiac adverse effect.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q20 (PDF p. 158)
questions.quote: Adverse effects include palpitations, bradycardia, an irregular heartbeat, difficulty breathing, signs of heart failure, and cold hands and feet.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.situation: Mr. Reyes, 50, had a liver transplant 3 months ago. He is on immunosuppressants to prevent organ rejection and comes to the transplant clinic for follow-up.
questions.stem: He takes tacrolimus daily. Which finding suggests an ADVERSE effect of the drug?
questions.rationale: Tacrolimus can cause nephrotoxicity, shown by rising serum creatinine and decreasing urine output, as well as pleural effusion. Hypertension, not hypotension, is a common side effect.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q22 (PDF p. 161)
questions.quote: Nephrotoxicity is characterized by an increasing serum creatinine level and a decrease in urine output.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.situation: Mr. Reyes, 50, had a liver transplant 3 months ago. He is on immunosuppressants to prevent organ rejection and comes to the transplant clinic for follow-up.
questions.stem: He is also on cyclosporine. Which laboratory finding is an adverse effect of cyclosporine?
questions.rationale: Cyclosporine adverse effects include nephrotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, infection, hypertension, tremor, hirsutism, hypomagnesemia, hyperkalemia, and hyperglycemia.
explanations: Correct: hyperkalemia can occur with cyclosporine.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q100 (PDF p. 249)
questions.quote: Additionally, neurotoxicity, gastrointestinal effects, hyperkalemia, and hyperglycemia can occur.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client on torsemide, a loop diuretic, has new lab results. Which value suggests an adverse effect of the drug?
questions.rationale: Loop diuretics can cause profound water and electrolyte loss. Normal potassium is 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L, so 3.1 mEq/L shows depletion. The other values are within normal limits.
explanations: At the low end of normal.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q32 (PDF p. 171)
questions.quote: the normal potassium level is 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0 mmol/L).

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client is receiving IV tobramycin every 8 hours. Which finding should the nurse report as a possible adverse effect?
questions.rationale: Aminoglycosides are nephrotoxic (rising BUN and creatinine), ototoxic (tinnitus, hearing loss), and neurotoxic.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q50 (PDF p. 190)
questions.quote: nephrotoxicity as evidenced by an increased BUN and serum creatinine; irreversible ototoxicity

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client has taken a calcium channel blocker for hypertension for 2 months. Which finding suggests drug tolerance has developed?
questions.rationale: Tolerance to an antihypertensive shows as rising blood pressure readings despite therapy. The provider may adjust the dose, change the drug, or add a diuretic.
explanations: Correct: rising BP despite therapy shows tolerance.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q55 (PDF p. 196)
questions.quote: Drug tolerance can develop in a client taking an antihypertensive such as a calcium channel blocker, which is evident by rising blood pressure levels.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Before giving hydroxyzine by intramuscular injection, what should the nurse tell the client?
options: 'You may feel some pain at the injection site.'
questions.rationale: Hydroxyzine is an antiemetic and sedative. The IM injection can be painful. It causes dry mouth and drowsiness, and IM drugs take about 20 to 30 minutes to work.
explanations: It causes dry mouth, not salivation.
IM onset is about 20 to 30 minutes.
Correct: the injection can be painful.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q70 (PDF p. 215)
questions.quote: The injection can be painful. Hydroxyzine causes dry mouth and drowsiness as side effects.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A child is brought to the emergency room after swallowing many paracetamol (acetaminophen) tablets. Which antidote does the nurse prepare?
questions.rationale: Acetylcysteine is the antidote for acetaminophen overdose. Vitamin K reverses warfarin, protamine reverses heparin, and succimer treats lead poisoning.
explanations: Vitamin K is the antidote for warfarin.
Protamine is the antidote for heparin.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q75 (PDF p. 220)
questions.quote: Acetylcysteine is the antidote for acetaminophen overdose.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: IV potassium chloride is prescribed for a client with hypokalemia. Which action is correct?
options: Give it as a slow IV push
Dilute it and give it by infusion pump
Use a filter in the IV line
Apply cold compresses to the IV site
questions.rationale: Potassium chloride irritates veins and must be diluted and given with an infusion pump. It is never given by IV push or bolus, which can cause cardiac arrest.
explanations: Never give potassium by push; it can cause cardiac arrest.
Correct: dilute and use a pump.
A filter is not needed for potassium.
Cold constricts the vein and adds irritation.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q110 (PDF p. 259)
questions.quote: Potassium chloride is never administered as a bolus injection because it can cause cardiac arrest.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Ondansetron is prescribed for a client receiving chemotherapy. By which route does the nurse expect it to be given for chemotherapy-induced nausea?
questions.rationale: Ondansetron comes in oral, IM, and IV forms. The IV route is used for nausea relief in clients receiving chemotherapy.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q125 (PDF p. 275)
questions.quote: The IV route is the route used when relief of nausea is needed in the client receiving chemotherapy.

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of Mother with Complications of Childbearing
questions.situation: Aling Joy, G2P1 at 35 weeks, is admitted with severe preeclampsia and started on a magnesium sulfate infusion.
questions.stem: Which medication must the nurse keep at the bedside during the infusion?
questions.rationale: Calcium gluconate is the antidote for magnesium sulfate toxicity and is kept at the bedside throughout the infusion.
explanations: Correct: the antidote for magnesium toxicity.
Oxytocin stimulates contractions; it is not an antidote.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q141 (PDF p. 291)
questions.quote: Calcium gluconate is the antidote to magnesium sulfate.

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of Mother with Complications of Childbearing
questions.situation: Aling Joy, G2P1 at 35 weeks, is admitted with severe preeclampsia and started on a magnesium sulfate infusion.
questions.stem: Why should the nurse check Aling Joy often for signs of labor while she is on magnesium sulfate?
options: Magnesium raises the risk of infection
Its sedative effect may keep her from noticing labor
Labor always starts within hours of the drug
questions.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is a CNS depressant and anticonvulsant. Its sedative effect may keep the client from perceiving labor, so the nurse checks for signs of labor.
explanations: Magnesium relaxes, rather than stimulates, the uterus.
Infection risk is not increased by this drug.
Correct: sedation can mask the onset of labor.
Labor onset is not predictable from the drug.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q141 (PDF p. 291)
questions.quote: Because of the sedative effect of the magnesium sulfate, the client may not perceive labor.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which finding is a common dose-related side effect of beta-adrenergic blockers?
questions.rationale: Dose-related side effects of beta blockers include dizziness from hypotension, bradycardia, and sexual dysfunction.
explanations: Fatigue, not more energy, is common.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q156 (PDF p. 306)
questions.quote: Side effects commonly associated with beta blockers are usually dose related and include dizziness (hypotensive effect), bradycardia, hypotension, and sexual dysfunction

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease is started on epoetin alfa. Which supplement is needed for the drug to work fully?
questions.rationale: Epoetin stimulates red cell production, which needs iron. Without iron the client does not get the full benefit. Hypertension is a side effect of epoetin.
explanations: Not required for red cell production.
Not required for red cell production.
Correct: iron is needed to make red cells.
Not required for red cell production.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q190 (PDF p. 344)
questions.quote: Iron is needed for RBC production; otherwise, the body cannot produce sufficient erythrocytes.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A client suddenly stopped long-term benzodiazepine therapy. Which findings of withdrawal should the nurse expect?
options: Excessive sleepiness and low blood pressure
questions.rationale: Benzodiazepine withdrawal causes tremor, sweating, agitation, nervousness, insomnia, anorexia, and cramps. After high-dose use it can progress to delirium, hypertension, and seizures.
explanations: Lethargy is not part of withdrawal.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q195 (PDF p. 349)
questions.quote: Withdrawal symptoms include tremor, sweating, agitation, nervousness, insomnia, anorexia, and muscular cramps.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client asks why the first dose of prazosin must be taken at bedtime. The nurse explains that the first dose may cause:
options: Sudden dizziness or fainting from low BP
questions.rationale: Prazosin, an alpha blocker, can cause a 'first-dose' hypotensive reaction with dizziness, lightheadedness, and possible fainting. It is better tolerated if the client is already in bed.
explanations: Not the reason for bedtime dosing.
Not the reason for bedtime dosing.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q208 (PDF p. 363)
questions.quote: “First-dose hypotensive reaction” may occur during early therapy, which is characterized by dizziness, lightheadedness, and possible loss of consciousness.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Furosemide 40 mg IV is given to a client with dyspnea from pulmonary congestion. One hour later, which finding BEST shows the drug achieved its purpose?
questions.rationale: Here furosemide was given to reduce preload and relieve pulmonary congestion. Clear lungs show that purpose was met; more urine is expected but is not the goal itself.
explanations: Correct: shows the congestion has resolved.
Expected, but not the therapeutic goal.
Not the goal of the therapy.
Not the goal of the therapy.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q215 (PDF p. 370)
questions.quote: it was given to decrease preload and reduce the pulmonary congestion and associated difficulty in breathing.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: During an IV amphotericin B infusion for histoplasmosis, the nurse should monitor closely for:
options: A sudden large increase in urine
questions.rationale: Amphotericin B is toxic. It can cause chills, fever, headache, vomiting, and impaired renal function (decreased urine output) during infusion, and it irritates veins, often causing thrombophlebitis.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q233 (PDF p. 388)
questions.quote: can produce symptoms during administration such as chills, fever (hyperthermia), headache, vomiting, and impaired renal function

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client on hemodialysis takes enalapril daily. When should the nurse give the dose on a dialysis day?
questions.rationale: Antihypertensives are given after hemodialysis. This prevents hypotension during dialysis and prevents the drug from being removed by dialysis.
explanations: Risks hypotension, and the drug is dialyzed out.
Risks hypotension, and the drug is dialyzed out.
Skipping a day leaves BP uncontrolled.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q257 (PDF p. 414)
questions.quote: Antihypertensive medications, such as enalapril, are administered to the client after hemodialysis.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client on a thiazide diuretic is monitored for hypokalemia. Which ECG finding is expected?
questions.rationale: Hypokalemia (below 3.5 mEq/L) causes ST depression, inverted T waves, a prominent U wave, and heart block, plus hyporeflexia, muscle weakness, and hypoactive bowel sounds.
explanations: Correct: a classic sign of hypokalemia.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q268 (PDF p. 425)
questions.quote: ECG abnormalities such as ST depression, inverted T wave, prominent U wave, and heart block.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Before giving procainamide, an antidysrhythmic, what should the nurse do FIRST?
options: Check the blood pressure and pulse
Schedule a drug level for next week
questions.rationale: BP and pulse are checked before procainamide because it can cause toxic cardiac effects. Serum levels are also monitored (therapeutic level 4 to 10 mcg/mL).
explanations: Correct: assess BP and pulse before giving it.
Levels are monitored, but this does not protect the current dose.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q270 (PDF p. 427)
questions.quote: Before the medication is administered, the client’s blood pressure and pulse are checked.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: How should the nurse instruct a client to take oral bisacodyl for the fastest effect?
questions.rationale: Bisacodyl works fastest on an empty stomach. Taken at bedtime it acts by morning. Milk and antacids can dissolve the enteric coating early.
explanations: Milk can dissolve the coating and does not speed the effect.
Correct: an empty stomach gives the most rapid effect.
Antacids also damage the enteric coating.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q275 (PDF p. 432)
questions.quote: The most rapid effect from bisacodyl occurs when it is taken on an empty stomach.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client on digoxin has a serum level of 2.3 ng/mL. Which complaint is consistent with this level?
questions.rationale: The therapeutic range is 0.8 to 2.0 ng/mL. Toxicity causes anorexia, nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, photophobia, and visual changes such as halos around bright objects.
explanations: Correct: visual disturbance is a sign of toxicity.
Not a sign of digoxin toxicity.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q287 (PDF p. 446)
questions.quote: The therapeutic range is 0.8 to 2.0 ng/mL (1.02 to 2.56 nmol/L).

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client on a heparin infusion has a PTT of 65 seconds (control 30 seconds). What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: The therapeutic PTT for heparin is 1.5 to 2.5 times the control (45 to 75 seconds here), so 65 seconds is therapeutic.
explanations: The value is therapeutic, not excessive.
Protamine is for excessive anticoagulation or bleeding.
Correct: the PTT is in the therapeutic range.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q290 (PDF p. 450)
questions.quote: Desired range for therapeutic anticoagulation is 1.5 to 2.5 times the control.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which instruction should the nurse give a client starting levothyroxine for hypothyroidism?
options: Take it in the morning before breakfast
Take it at bedtime to avoid drowsiness
Skip doses on days the pulse is fast
questions.rationale: Levothyroxine is taken in the morning before breakfast, at the same time daily, to prevent insomnia. Replacement is lifelong, and the client monitors the pulse and reports chest pain.
explanations: A fast pulse is reported, not managed by skipping doses.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q294 (PDF p. 456)
questions.quote: take the medication in the morning before breakfast to prevent insomnia

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client with diabetes insipidus is on intranasal desmopressin. Which parameter BEST shows that the drug is effective?
questions.rationale: Desmopressin is an antidiuretic hormone analog. Its effect is judged by fluid balance: intake and output, daily weight, and edema.
explanations: Not the main measure of effect.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q339 (PDF p. 507)
questions.quote: Fluid status can be evaluated by noting intake and urine output, daily weight, and the presence of edema.
